detail: supported

It differs from its sibling [Tile-Based Solid Voxelization](9087-tile-based-solid-voxelization.md) by grouping work by input primitive (triangles) rather than by spatial location (tiles), which incurs warp underutilization and high memory bandwidth/atomic serialization costs compared to tile-based methods [S2].

The evidence explicitly describes the 'Direct, triangle-parallel solid voxelization' algorithm as parallelizing over all triangles (grouping work by input primitive). It explicitly states that this approach has two main weaknesses: 1) 'the number of relevant voxel columns can vary significantly among the triangles processed by one warp, leading to underutilization' (warp underutilization), and 2) 'flipping all voxels in the derived x range poses high memory bandwidth requirements. Moreover, many atomic operations may have to be sequentialized' (high memory bandwidth/atomic serialization costs). The text contrasts this with the 'tile-based method' introduced in section 4.2 to 'elude the shortcomings of the triangle-parallel method'. Thus, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported

*   **Triangle Data:** For each triangle, the algorithm computes the bounding box in the YZ plane and the plane equation of the triangle [S2, G].

The claim states that the algorithm computes the bounding box in the YZ plane AND the plane equation of the triangle. The evidence (Source [S2]) explicitly confirms that the algorithm determines the 'bounding box in the yz plane'. However, the evidence does not state that the algorithm computes the 'plane equation of the triangle'. Instead, it mentions projecting the center 'onto the triangle's plane' and using edge functions defined by edge normals and distances. While the plane equation is implicitly used for the projection step, the text does not claim that the plane equation itself is computed as a distinct output or step in the same manner as the bounding box. Therefore, only part of the claim is explicitly supported.
unsupported
*   **When to use:** When the number of triangles is moderate and the grid size is small to medium, or when simplicity of implementation is prioritized over maximum performance [S2].

The claim states that the evidence supports using the algorithm when 'simplicity of implementation is prioritized over maximum performance'. However, Source [S2] explicitly identifies 'warp underutilization' and 'high memory bandwidth/atomic serialization costs' as main weaknesses of the triangle-parallel approach, particularly for large grids. While the algorithm is described as 'direct' and 'simple' in structure (one thread per triangle), the text does not claim that simplicity is the reason for its use, nor does it suggest it is the preferred choice when simplicity is prioritized over performance. In fact, the text introduces a 'tile-based' approach specifically to 'elude the shortcomings' of the triangle-parallel method, implying that the triangle-parallel method is not the optimal choice for performance, but also does not frame it as the 'simple' alternative to be chosen for that reason. The claim adds a specific justification ('simplicity... prioritized') that is not present in the evidence.
unsupported

Direct, triangle-parallel solid voxelization is a data-parallel algorithm that determines all voxels inside a closed, watertight mesh by processing every triangle in parallel, dedicating one thread per triangle [S1, S2].

The claim states that direct, triangle-parallel solid voxelization is a data-parallel algorithm that determines all voxels inside a closed, watertight mesh by processing every triangle in parallel, dedicating one thread per triangle. Source [S2] explicitly defines this method in Section 4.1 as 'Direct, triangle-parallel solid voxelization' and states: 'we parallelize over all triangles, dedicating one thread per triangle.' It further describes the process of determining voxels inside the object (solid voxelization). Source [S1] also describes a 'triangle-parallel conservative voxelization' that processes 'all triangles in parallel, launching one thread per triangle.' While [S1] focuses on conservative voxelization and [S2] on solid voxelization, the core architectural description (data-parallel, one thread per triangle) matches the claim perfectly, and [S2] explicitly links this parallelization strategy to the 'direct, triangle-parallel' approach for solid voxelization.
supported
Each bit corresponds to a voxel $(i, j, k)$ in the grid, where $0 \le i < n_x$, $0 \le j < n_y$, $0 \le k < n_z$ [S2].

The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states in Section 4.1: 'The resulting x coordinate q in voxel space, where each voxel (i, j, k), 0 ≤ i < n*x, is of size 13...'. Although the text contains some OCR artifacts (e.g., 'n*x' instead of 'n_x', '13' likely meaning '1' or a formatting error for dimensions), it clearly defines the voxel indexing with coordinates (i, j, k) and specifies the range for the first dimension as 0 to n_x (represented as n*x). The claim accurately reflects this definition of the grid and voxel correspondence found in the text.

It solves the problem of generating a dense voxel grid representation of a mesh on a GPU by projecting triangles onto the YZ plane, testing voxel columns for overlap, and using atomic operations to set the interior bits along the X axis [S2].

The claim accurately describes the algorithm presented in Source [S2] for direct, triangle-parallel solid voxelization. The source explicitly states that the algorithm processes triangles in parallel, determines the bounding box in the YZ plane, loops over voxel columns, tests for overlap using edge functions, projects along the X-axis, and uses atomic operations (specifically atomic xor) to set/flip bits for the interior voxels along the X-axis.
supported

# Initialize voxel grid as a flat array of 32-bit integers [S1]

The evidence explicitly states that 'Voxel state is encoded by a single bit in a linear array' and mentions handling '32-bit value' updates. A linear array where each voxel is represented by a single bit within a 32-bit integer word is effectively a flat array of 32-bit integers. The claim accurately reflects this data structure description found in the source.
